session_meta.research_objective:
Focus group guide exploring how men in the UK make everyday food
choices, how social context, work, hobbies, health, taste and other
people shape what they eat, how gender and masculinity may influence
food choices, and what would need to change for plant-based foods to
become more acceptable or appealing.
session_meta.topic_domain: Masculinity, food choice, animal product consumption, and plant-based eating
session_meta.participant_collective_identity: Men in the UK reflecting on food choices, male friendship, gender norms, and plant-based eating
session_meta.moderator_knowledge_brief:
Explore (1) everyday food decision-making, (2) the social contexts in
which men spend time with male friends, (3) the influence of other
people, work, hobbies, health, nutrition and taste on food choices,
(4) whether participants perceive gender as shaping what they eat,
(5) social acceptability and gendered meanings attached to vegetarian,
vegan, plant-based, feminine or masculine foods, and (6) what personal,
social and practical changes would make plant-based eating more viable
or appealing. The discussion should remain exploratory, non-judgmental,
and non-leading.

initial_session_plan.thematisation_approach: These are three British men in their early-to-mid fifties, from different parts of England, all self-identified meat eaters. I will frame them as people with real, lived daily experience of food — shopping, cooking, eating out, eating with others — and treat that ordinary, practical experience as the resource we're here to draw on. I won't foreground gender or masculinity in the framing; those themes will emerge from the discussion itself.
priority_research_areas: Whether and how gender/masculinity shapes food choices — participants are likely to initially deny or minimise this, requiring careful behavioural grounding and patience before authentic views emerge
Social acceptability of plant-based eating among men — high risk of socially performative answers; need to anchor responses in specific social situations rather than abstract attitudes
What would genuinely need to change for plant-based eating to be viable — easy to produce vague or aspirational answers; probe should push toward concrete personal and social barriers
The relationship between male friendship contexts and food choices — the bridge section (Section 1→3) that may unlock tacit norms without participants having to name them as 'gender'

participant_notes.anticipated_role: Urban, North West — likely familiar with diverse food culture; may be more open to nuance on plant-based eating. At 53, possibly health-conscious. Watch for whether he becomes an early opinion-setter that others defer to.
participant_notes.initial_attention_flag: Monitor for dominance — if he takes strong early positions, others may self-censor

participant_notes.anticipated_role: Suburban, South East — may reflect more conventional middle-England food norms. Could be thoughtful and measured. Possible moderate voice in the group.

Rural, East of England — likely strongest connection to traditional food culture, farming, countryside identity. Most likely to have unreflective attachment to meat as natural or normal. May be less forthcoming initially.
participant_notes.initial_attention_flag: Watch for reticence; rural/village identity may make him feel less represented in the group; worth a warm early invite if he goes quiet

known_risk_conditions: Topic may produce socially desirable answers on gender — men this age may feel pressure to appear 'modern' by denying that gender influences their choices; use behavioural grounding (specific past meals, specific social moments) rather than abstract opinion questions
Group may converge quickly on 'it's about taste, not gender' — plan a sharpening move that ties food to a specific social context (e.g. eating in front of other men) to break the surface
Plant-based section may produce performative scepticism or blokey dismissiveness — avoid letting this harden unchallenged; invite dissent or probe for any positive experience without leading
All three are meat eaters — there is no internal diversity on dietary identity; consensus risk on meat-positive, plant-negative positions is structurally elevated throughout
Three-person group is small — one dominant voice can easily crowd out the others; track airtime carefully across all sections
initial_session_plan.directivity_plan: Sections 0–2 (intro and context): light touch. Build rapport, get them talking to each other, don't push on sensitive ground yet. Let food preferences and social habits surface naturally. Section 3 (gender and food): moderate to firm. Initial answers will likely be dismissive; be patient but use behavioural grounding and contradiction-reflection if denial is too smooth. Sections 4–5 (plant-based): firm but non-coercive. These are the research heart of the session; push for specificity on barriers and changes, invite dissent if scepticism hardens into group consensus. Section 6 (closing): light — brief, warm, genuinely open invitation, don't reopen closed ground.

time_budget.budget_rationale: Main topic sections (3, 4, 5) carry the research weight and receive the largest share. Context sections (1, 2) are warm-up and bridge material — useful but not the destination. Intro (0) and closing (6) are kept tight. Sections 4 and 5 are given slightly more than Section 3 because they involve more imaginative and speculative work that typically takes longer to develop.

discussion_guide.scripted_question:
Hi everyone, thanks so much for joining the focus group today. We’re
going to take about 45 minutes to talk about your food choices and
opinions, and this will be recorded for research purposes. Try not to
overthink the questions, and simply speak freely. There are no right
or wrong answers. Please be respectful of your fellow focus group
members, and keep your responses relatively brief to allow time for
everyone to speak. But remember that this is a conversation, not an
interview, so you can jump in when you have something to say and you
don’t have to take turns answering each question, but you can if you
want to. Okay great, let’s start by going around and saying your name
and where in the UK you’re coming from today.

section_summaries.discussion_summary: This section was introductory — participants established geographic and contextual diversity (urban fringe, rural East Anglia, suburban North West), with brief signals that setting shapes social experience. No substantive themes emerged yet beyond orientation. The moderator's closing question pivoted toward the session's core territory: where men gather with male friends and what makes those places meaningful.
section_summaries.strategy_summary: The priority here was low-friction entry — names, locations, no pressure. Letting participants introduce themselves voluntarily worked smoothly; all three contributed without prompting. The transition question was deliberately concrete and experiential to lower the bar for the first substantive answer. Too early to assess whether the approach is drawing out the right depth, but the room feels open.

section_summaries.section_label: Opening discussion: male friendship and place
section_summaries.discussion_summary: This section centered on a productive tension between convenience and depth — whether the frictionlessness of a default gathering spot enables regular connection or forecloses meaningful conversation. Urban commuter logic (the station pub as passive glue) was contrasted with rural intentionality (planned effort yielding presence and depth). Gregor usefully complicated the binary, resisting romanticisation of either mode and introducing mood and occasion as variables. The section closed with a natural pivot toward food decision-making.
section_summaries.strategy_summary: James and Mark developed a genuine exchange organically, so I held back and let it run — the tension between convenience and depth was substantive enough to be worth sustaining. My only intervention was pulling in Gregor, who had been silent; his response added useful nuance without derailing the thread. The transition to food was clean given natural momentum. The main risk was letting James and Mark's bilateral exchange run slightly long before including Gregor, but the payoff justified it.

section_summaries.discussion_summary: This section centred on habit, familiarity, and cultural embeddedness as the real drivers of meat-eating — with participants distinguishing between unreflective autopilot and comfortable, acknowledged default. A productive tension emerged between Gregor's initial framing of pure practicality and James's push toward recognising unseen cultural scaffolding; Gregor conceded the point without defensiveness. Mark largely confirmed the consensus. The section closed with the moderator pivoting toward gender as an explanatory frame.
section_summaries.strategy_summary: I stayed largely absent while Gregor and James developed a genuinely useful exchange — James's gentle challenge and Gregor's concession was worth letting run without interruption. I pulled in Mark when he'd been silent too long; his contribution confirmed the pattern but added little new texture, suggesting I could have pushed him earlier or harder. The transition question on gender was clean and well-timed, opening a new angle without forcing it.

section_summaries.discussion_summary: This section deepened the gender-and-meat thread by distinguishing two complementary mechanisms: inherited cultural identity (farming lineage, rural baseline) and a more diffuse masculine norm against introspection — the idea that examining one's own food choices reads as fussy, precious, or threatening. Participants converged on the 'tight box' framing: genuine enjoyment of meat is unproblematic, but acknowledging the social scaffolding around it carries social risk. The section ended with a productive reframe — cultural awareness and genuine preference as non-exclusive.
section_summaries.strategy_summary: I stayed absent while Mark and Gregor developed a genuinely productive bilateral exchange, then intervened to pull James in once the tight-box framing had crystallised — timing the inclusion so he could respond to a concrete idea rather than an open vacuum. That worked well; his contribution sharpened rather than repeated the theme. The transition question — imagining a plant-based switch — was designed to move from diagnosis toward practical friction, a clean pivot given the momentum.

section_summaries.discussion_summary: This section examined the friction of imagined dietary change, with a productive tension between practical barriers (cooking knowledge, rural access, social visibility) and the psychological architecture beneath them — incuriosity as a form of self-protection. Gregor challenged Mark's obstacle-framing directly; Mark partially conceded but defended the particularity of rural social context. James synthesised both positions usefully, naming habit and comfort as the deeper mechanism and loosening the idea that current eating patterns are inevitable.
section_summaries.strategy_summary: I stayed absent through the Mark-Gregor exchange, which was substantive enough to sustain without intervention — the direct challenge and partial concession was worth letting resolve. I pulled James in once the exchange had crystallised rather than opened, so he could respond to something concrete; his bridging role worked well and landed the section's sharpest observation. The transition question built directly on his 'not inevitable' framing, which was clean. No significant missteps, though I could have probed Mark's rural-context claim harder.

section_summaries.discussion_summary: This section reached the session's sharpest moment of self-examination: participants moved from diagnosing external barriers to interrogating their own relationship to curiosity and choice. A productive distinction crystallised between conscious comfort (knowing what you'd miss and accepting it) and pre-emptive closure (shutting down enquiry before it becomes risky). The section complicated easy self-awareness too — James noting that Gregor's honesty had quickly become a vantage point for advising others, rather than sustained discomfort.
section_summaries.strategy_summary: I intervened sparingly — twice, both to pull in quieter voices once the active exchange had reached a natural pause. Holding back while Gregor's self-correction unfolded was the right call; interrupting would have foreclosed something genuinely valuable. Timing James's inclusion well paid off — he complicated Gregor's newly settled position rather than simply affirming it. The closing question was clean and low-pressure. No significant missteps; the section resolved itself more fully than most.

section_summaries.discussion_summary: This section offered a closing consolidation rather than new territory: Mark reasserted the reality of his social context as a genuine constraint rather than avoidance, while also claiming conscious contentment with his choices — separating the 'shut down curiosity' charge from the legitimacy of his lived situation. The section's modest contribution was anchoring a distinction the group had circled: that acknowledging pre-emptive closure doesn't automatically invalidate the underlying preference or social reality.
section_summaries.strategy_summary: With only one participant turn before closing, there was little to moderate — the section was effectively a wrap. Affirming Mark's closing statement before opening a final round was low-risk and appropriate given time constraints. The affirmation ('No, Mark, you really don't') was perhaps slightly too validating given the session had productively pressured his position; a more neutral handoff might have preserved the group's critical momentum through to the end. No significant missteps given the context.
